newsitem.title: CROATIA: U.S. envoy warns Croatia over treatment of Serbs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy warns Croatia over treatment of Serbs.

text.p: U.S. ambassador Peter Galbraith on Tuesday rammed home the message that Croatia would not win entry to Western institutions unless it allowed all displaced minority Serbs to return home and live in safety.

"The United States will support Croatia's integration into Western institutions, including Partnership for Peace, NATO and the European Union. But there are preconditions," Galbraith, ambassador to Croatia since 1993, told a news conference.
"Specifically, these conditions include Croatia permitting the return of all refugees and displaced persons to their homes."

Senior Croatian officials visited Washington last week and held intensive talks with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, who scolded Foreign Minister Mate Granic over Croatia's treatment of Serbs and other peace accord violations.
Granic later challenged the U.S. State Department's description of the meeting and said the two had agreed on "more than 90 percent" of the issues they discussed.
But Galbraith said the United States policy towards Zagreb is "unambiguous and clear".

"Croatia will go no further in the process of integration into (the West) unless and until all Croatian Serbs who wish to return to Croatia are able to do so, and this includes Serbs who are currently in Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina."
He said Albright was appalled by a recent incident in the Kostajnica area when Bosnian Croat refugees, resettled in the area, harassed and expelled local elderly Serbs.
"It was not an accidental outbreak of violence but evidently something that was organised. It was unacceptable," Galbraith said.

"It is clear that a state that is not sufficiently strong to create security for its own people is not a state that could qualify for admission to NATO or the European Union," he added in his strongest public criticism of Zagreb so far.

Up to 200,000 Serbs fled the Croatian army recapture of their rebel Krajina enclave in the summer of 1995. Some 60,000 of them settled in the last Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia, now administered by the United Nations Transitional Authority (UNTAES).

The current U.N. mandate in the enclave expires on July 15, when Zagreb wants to take full control. But Galbraith said: "The return of the Serbs will affect our view on the extension of the UNTAES mandate."

Zagreb has issued a general amnesty and guaranteed safety to Serbs wishing to go back home. The few who have actually returned have found their property destroyed and their houses occupied by Croatian refugees.

Croatia is very keen to return some 80,000 of its own refugees to Eastern Slavonia, from where they were expelled by separatist Serbs who oppossed Croatia's drive for independence from federal Yugoslavia in 1991.

That means Serb refugees in the enclave would have to move out of Croatian houses there and return to their homes in the Krajina. Zagreb, in coordination with the United Nations, has devised plans for a large-scale return of all refugees.
"The issue of return is critical to the whole peace process...If the return doesn't occur here (in Croatia), it probably won't occur anywhere," Galbraith said.
